---
title: "The Bit"
---

### The Bit

The fundamental unit of information is the **bit** — the distinction between two equally probable possibilities: $0$ or $1$, yes or no, heads or tails. Any two-state physical system encodes exactly one bit: a spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ particle, a photon polarization, a transistor switch.

A system with $n$ bits has $N = 2^n$ distinguishable states. Conversely, a system with $N$ states encodes:

$$n = \log_2 N \text{ bits}$$

This holds for non-integer values too: a three-state system encodes $\log_2 3 \approx 1.58$ bits.

A useful approximation: $2^{10} \approx 10^3$, so every 10 bits multiplies the state space by roughly $10^3$.

| $n$ (bits) | $N$ (states) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2 |
| 10 | 1,024 |
| 300 | $\approx 10^{90}$ |

> The observable universe contains $\sim 10^{90}$ particles. So **300 bits suffice to label every particle in the universe**. Human DNA, by contrast, encodes $\sim 6 \times 10^9$ bits — far exceeding what is needed for labeling alone.

---

### Information is Physical

Every bit is realized by a physical system. This has a deep consequence: physical limits constrain how much information any region of space can contain. The maximum information capacity of the observable universe is:

$$N_{\text{max}} \sim 10^{120} \text{ bits}$$

This follows from quantum mechanics and is finite — large, but bounded.
